newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: UN disarmament body may tackle landmines ban.
newsitem.headline: UN disarmament body may tackle landmines ban.

text.p: A U.N.-backed disarmament conference adopted a 1997 agenda on Friday which could lead to negotiations on a global ban on landmines, its president said.
But Joun Yung Sun, South Korea's ambassador and current president, conceded that the landmines issue remained divisive.
He said a formal consensus would still be required among the 61 member states before they could enter into actual negotiations to ban the lethal weapons -- blamed for killing 25,000 people a year.
"A consensus was reached on a draft agenda. It did not come easily," Joun told a news briefing.
"The agenda is the basis for developing a concrete work programme. There is much more work to do in the future."
Agreement on a 1997 agenda came after nearly a month of haggling in the United Nations-sponsored talks. The forum had been paralysed since opening a two-month session on January 21.
Diplomats welcomed the procedural breakthrough, but said tough negotiations on the substantive issues were ahead.
Some Western envoys still feared the landmine issue would be hostage to demands by non-aligned states for major powers to take bold steps toward total elimination of nuclear weapons.
Joun said: "Some states strongly insisted on having landmines on the agenda but other delegations did not want to see any place given on an official document to landmines."
More than 100 million landmines lie buried in countries around the world and are blamed for killing or maiming 25,000 people a year. Most are civilians and many are children.

Western states have a twin agenda at the Geneva talks. They favour pushing ahead with negotiations to halt production of fissile material (plutonium and highly-enriched uranium) and are also seeking a global landmines ban.

But India and Pakistan are leading a non-aligned campaign to force the five declared nuclear powers (Britain, China, France, Russia and the United States) to set up a committee to negotiate total nuclear disarmament within a set timetable.
Only then would the non-aligned be prepared to enter into fissile and landmines negotiations, according to diplomats.
The agenda adopted on Friday, virtually identical to the one adopted a year ago, is deliberately short on specifics and is broad enough to please everyone, according to diplomats.
"The agenda allows new topics to be put in under existing agenda items," a Western diplomat told Reuters.

For instance, landmines could be negotiated under the heading "comprehensive programme of disarmament". Other areas are nuclear disarmament and cessation of the nuclear arms race, under which fissile "cut-off" talks could be conducted.
Joun, asked whether landmines could be negotiated, replied: "Yes, if there is consensus. There is not one at the moment.
"If there is a consensus anything can be dealt with."
Canada is sponsoring its own 100-nation talks on a landmines treaty, but China is not taking part. Russia is attending the current session of the so-called "Ottawa process" in Vienna as an observer.

China and Russia are two top mines producers and exporters whose participation is deemed essential for a universal ban. Both are members of the Geneva forum, the world's sole multilateral disarmament body which last year negotiated a nuclear test ban.
